review_basis: Visually inspected all sixteen original numbered WebP slides directly from GitHub, following actual layout, graphs, flows, labels and worked examples. Topic-first scenes use verified source order.
part_title: Model Explainability, Decision Trees and Human Oversight

scenes.title: Interpretability and Performance Trade-offs
scenes.narration: The left panel shows a simple decision tree with rules that are easy to trace. The right panel shows a densely connected neural network that can capture more complicated patterns but may require post-hoc explanation methods. The center contains the actual decision criteria: measure both models on the same validation dataset using appropriate metrics, then assess what level of explanation stakeholders and regulations require. There is no universal rule that complexity means greater accuracy, or that interpretability must always sacrifice prediction quality. In the loan example below, explainability matters because a reviewer must understand the factors affecting an applicant. Choose based on measured quality, explanation needs, fairness and business constraints, rather than selecting the most sophisticated-looking model.

scenes.title: Explaining Decisions with Decision Trees
scenes.narration: Follow the credit-risk diagram from the root at the top: is annual income greater than fifty thousand dollars? The yes branch goes left, the no branch goes right. Each side then tests whether the applicant has a good credit history. Read the four resulting leaves: higher income and good credit history lead to low risk; higher income and poor history lead to medium risk; lower income and good history lead to medium risk; and lower income with poor history leads to high risk. Now trace the bottom worked example. An applicant has eighty thousand dollars of annual income and good credit history, so the answers are yes, then yes, reaching the green low-risk leaf. These are illustrative model rules, not real lending criteria. Decision trees are explainable because a reviewer can inspect each split, although an overly deep tree may overfit training data.

scenes.title: Partial Dependence Plots
scenes.narration: Follow the numbered steps across the top. Start with a trained model and observed dataset. Select one feature, here price, and vary it across a range while holding the other features at each record's observed values. Generate predictions for every selected price, average those predictions across records, and plot the resulting curve. The lower graph labels the horizontal axis as price in US dollars and the vertical axis as average predicted demand. In this illustration, average predicted demand declines from roughly one hundred eighty at low price to around twenty-five at fifty dollars. This tells us about the model's average learned relationship, not proof that a change in price causes a change in demand. Correlated features can create unrealistic combinations and distort the plot. A PDP provides a useful global explanation, but it does not explain every individual prediction.

scenes.title: Human-Centered Design for Explainable AI
scenes.narration: Look at the four stages from left to right. Customer application data enters an ML model, which produces a recommendation. The next panel displays the suggested approval with understandable reasons: steady income, low debt and a long employment history. Notice its medium confidence indicator; that is not a guarantee of correctness. The third panel gives a trained reviewer the explanation, the uncertainty and a checklist to assess potential bias and relevant context. Finally, the reviewer may confirm, adjust or escalate the decision. The principles at the top are clarity, unbiased decisions, accountability and accessibility. The bottom loan-review example reinforces the same sequence. Human-centered design does not mean adding an approval button to an opaque model; it means giving people enough reliable information, control and escalation options to exercise meaningful oversight.
